analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying their former colleagues for life.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote after being referred to the House Judiciary Committee in February 2014, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, former senators must wait two years and former House members one year before lobbying Congress. This bill would replace those cooling-off periods with a total, permanent ban: anyone who has served in Congress could never make a lobbying contact with a member, officer, or employee of either chamber, or with covered executive branch officials, on pain of fines or prison. It would also bar former elected House officers from such contacts for one year. The ban would have applied to members leaving office after the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who currently share lawmakers with a revolving door of former colleagues paid to influence them. Sitting members also gain a workplace shielded from former colleagues returning as paid advocates.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the current cooling-off periods — two years for former senators, one year for former House members — with a lifetime ban on lobbying contacts with any member, officer, or employee of either chamber, punishable by fine or imprisonment [S2][S3].
The ban also covers lobbying contacts with covered executive branch officials, closing a route by which former lawmakers cash in on their government relationships [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who would lose access to the lucrative lobbying market their government service currently qualifies them for, and the lobbying firms and interest groups that hire them for that access.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban is broader than the existing cooling-off rules and broader than many state laws; critics of such bans argue it can go further than needed to prevent undue influence and may deter qualified people from seeking office at all.

The bill as introduced does not restrict the large share of congressional staff who also pass through the revolving door, and it leaves open indirect channels such as advising or strategizing behind a registered lobbyist, so its practical effect could be narrower than a full lifetime ban suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real conflict of interest: former lawmakers selling access to their former colleagues. The trade-off is fairness to individuals who leave public service versus a workplace less shaped by paid influence, and a total ban is a blunt instrument compared with the existing waiting periods. On balance it would directly serve the public's interest in a Congress that answers to voters rather than to former colleagues on a client roster, though its omission of senior staff limits how much of the revolving door it actually closes.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on February 6, 2014, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].

On March 20, 2014, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, which is the last action recorded; no hearing, markup, or vote followed [S5].
It drew one cosponsor, a Democrat, and never advanced out of committee before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying industry, which keep the current one- and two-year waiting periods rather than a lifetime ban; anyone they hire for access is no worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Former members of Congress and lobbying firms

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a lifetime lobbying ban on former members of Congress.

for.name: 1 House cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it attracted no other support in the chamber.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral; it sat in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and never reached a vote, so the record shows no Republican position either way.

industries.note: These firms pay former members largely for their relationships with sitting lawmakers; a lifetime ban would remove the most valuable hires from the market. Their interest in keeping the current rules runs against the public's interest in limiting paid access.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress (the revolving-door class)
industries.note: Former lawmakers command premium lobbying salaries because of their congressional ties; the bill would cut off that income stream entirely. Their interest in preserving the current waiting periods runs against the public's interest.
